readerTitle: Why medieval merchants could trust agents they never saw
caseNote: 실제 연구 (Greif의 마그레브 상인 연구, Axelrod의 반복 죄수의 딜레마 대회) + 실제 관찰 (eBay 평판 시스템) + 가상 적용 (수리 기사 고르기, 회사 안 팀 협업)
insight: 상대가 정직한 이유는 착해서가 아니라 미래의 거래가 남아 있고 다른 사람들이 지켜보기 때문이다. 신뢰를 만들려면 관계를 반복되게, 그리고 보이게 설계한다.
misconception: 사람을 믿을 수 있게 만드는 것은 계약서와 감시다. 한 번 손해 보더라도 정직하게 구는 건 순진한 선택이다.

sources.text: Greif, A. (1989). Reputation and Coalitions in Medieval Trade: Evidence on the Maghribi Traders. Journal of Economic History, 49(4).
Greif, A. (1993). Contract Enforceability and Economic Institutions in Early Trade: The Maghribi Traders' Coalition. American Economic Review, 83(3).
Axelrod, R. (1984). The Evolution of Cooperation. Basic Books.
Edwards, J. & Ogilvie, S. (2012). Contract enforcement, institutions, and social capital: the Maghribi traders reappraised. Economic History Review.
eBay feedback forum, introduced in 1996 (Pierre Omidyar's founder letter)

factChecks.note: 마그레브 상인(11세기 지중해, 카이로 게니자 문서) 연합이 부정을 저지른 대리인을 집단으로 고용하지 않았다는 해석은 Greif의 것입니다. Edwards & Ogilvie(2012)는 법원 등 공식 제도도 쓰였다고 반박했습니다. 카드 3에 'historians still debate'로 적었습니다.
Axelrod 대회: 1980년경 두 차례 컴퓨터 대회에서 Anatol Rapoport가 제출한 Tit for Tat가 모두 우승했다는 내용을 원문으로 다시 확인하세요.
eBay 피드백 제도의 도입 시기(1996년)를 게시 전에 확인하세요. 카드에는 수치를 넣지 않았습니다.
카드 5 계산(가상 수치): 정직한 거래 1회당 $100 × 앞으로 20회 = $2,000. 한 번 속여서 얻는 돈 $500. 2,000 > 500이므로 미래가 남아 있으면 정직이 이득. 마지막 거래에서는 잃을 미래가 $0이 되어 $500 > $0.

cards.title: Why medieval merchants could trust agents they never saw
body: In the 11th century, merchants in Egypt shipped goods across the Mediterranean to agents in Sicily and beyond. The agent sold the cargo and sent back the money.
No phone. No police reaching that far. An agent could simply keep the money. Most didn't.

image.label: A merchant ship crossing the sea between two harbours, with letters passing between them
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 지중해를 건너는 작은 중세 상선, 양쪽 항구에 상인과 대리인이 서 있고 그 사이로 편지 여러 통이 날아다니는 모습. 실제 깃발이나 문장은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which handyman will do the careful job?
body: Your bathroom needs retiling. Hidden shortcuts, like skipping waterproofing, won't show for a year. You have three quotes.
Who is most likely to do it properly?

options.text: The cheapest quote, from a crew working in town for one month
options.feedback: You save money now, but they have little to lose. By the time the leak shows, they're gone.

options.text: A local tiler who has done work for three neighbours in your building
options.feedback: Your neighbours are his next jobs. A shortcut on your floor could cost him the whole building. That's the idea in this lesson.

options.text: Anyone, as long as you sign a detailed contract with a guarantee
options.feedback: A contract helps, but enforcing it costs time and money. It works best alongside someone who wants your future business.

cards.title: Cheat one merchant, lose them all.
body: Economist Avner Greif studied letters these traders left behind. He found they worked as a loose group. They shared news about agents in their letters.
If an agent cheated one merchant, the whole group could stop hiring him. One stolen cargo could cost a lifetime of work.
Historians still debate how much this mattered next to courts. But the logic is clear: honesty paid because the future was worth more than one theft.

cards.title: Repeated games and reputation
body: In a **repeated game**, the same players meet again and again. Cheating today wins once, then costs every future deal. Economists call this the *shadow of the future*.
**Reputation** stretches the game further. When others can see how you behaved, cheating one partner costs you deals with all of them.
So cooperation doesn't need saints. It needs a future and an audience.

cards.title: Keep the cargo, or keep the career?
body: Twenty future trips outweigh one theft. But notice the last line: on the final trip, nothing is left to lose.

breakdown.label: Each honest trip
breakdown.detail: What an agent earns per job

breakdown.label: Future lost
breakdown.detail: 20 trips no one will give him

cards.softwareNote: eBay faced the same problem with strangers who would trade once. Its feedback scores, introduced in 1996, made each sale visible to every future buyer. A one-off sale became part of a repeated game.

cards.title: The simple strategy that kept winning.
body: Around 1980, political scientist Robert Axelrod ran computer tournaments. Programs played a repeated prisoner's dilemma against each other, many rounds each.
The winner was the simplest entry, called *Tit for Tat*: cooperate first, then copy whatever the other player did last.
It was **nice** (never cheated first), quick to punish cheating, and quick to forgive. In long games, that pattern earned trust and avoided being exploited.

image.label: Two players trading moves round after round, mostly cooperating
image.brief: 두 캐릭터가 여러 라운드에 걸쳐 카드를 주고받는 인포그래픽. 대부분 초록색 '협력' 카드, 한 번 빨간 '배신' 카드가 나오자 상대도 다음 라운드에 빨간 카드, 그 다음엔 다시 초록으로 돌아옴.

cards.title: Reputation fails when the game ends or no one sees.
body: When everyone knows it's the last round, the shadow of the future disappears. Watch for an employee about to leave, a supplier about to close, or a business being sold.
Reputation also needs an audience. If bad behaviour stays hidden, it costs nothing.
And trust is slow to build but quick to lose. One visible shortcut can undo years of good work.

cards.title: Now it's two teams in one company.
body: You lead the analytics team. The product team needs two of your people for a week to rescue a launch. Helping puts your own quarterly target at risk.
You'll work with the product team for years, and team leads talk. What do you do?

options.text: Decline politely. Your target is what you're measured on
options.feedback: You protect this quarter, but the product team and its friends will remember who didn't help. Future requests from you get slower answers.

options.text: Help, say clearly what it costs you, and ask for their support next time you need it
options.feedback: You cooperate first and make it visible, so it builds reputation. Naming the favour sets up reciprocity, like Tit for Tat.

options.text: Help quietly and never mention it
options.feedback: Generous, and it may build goodwill. But if no one sees it, and nothing is expected back, you risk becoming the team everyone leans on.

cards.title: People keep promises when the future is worth more than the shortcut.
body: To get trust, make the relationship long and the behaviour visible. To judge risk, ask who has a future with you and who doesn't.
**Try it today:** list one partner, supplier or colleague whose game with you is ending soon. What would you check more carefully now?
